text_blocks.snippet: A diminished or lost sense of taste, known as dysgeusia, can stem from various causes, including infections, medications, and even certain medical conditions. Damage to the nerves involved in taste perception, like from head injuries or surgeries, can also be a factor.
snippet_highlighted_words: infections, medications, and even certain medical conditions

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at potential causes:

list.snippet: Upper respiratory and middle ear infections: These can temporarily affect taste perception.

COVID-19: Loss of taste is a known symptom of COVID-19, and while most people regain their sense of taste after recovering, some may experience lingering issues, according to the National Institute on Aging.
Salivary gland infections: Infections of the salivary glands can also impact taste.
Antibiotics and antihistamines: These medications can cause dry mouth, which can alter taste.
Antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and bladder control medications: These can also contribute to dry mouth and taste changes.
Acid reflux (GERD): Stomach acid can irritate the mouth and affect taste perception, often causing a "brackish" or sour taste says the Boston Medical Center.
Diabetes, hypothyroidism, and kidney disease: These metabolic disorders can cause taste disturbances.
Neurological disorders: Conditions like multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's disease, and Parkinson's disease can affect taste perception.
Nutritional deficiencies: Deficiencies in zinc, vitamin B12, and folate can impact taste.
Cushing's syndrome: This hormonal disorder can also affect taste.
Oral hygiene and dental problems: Poor oral hygiene, gum disease, and issues with dentures can lead to taste changes.
Head and neck injuries: Trauma to the head or neck can damage nerves involved in taste.
Cancer treatments: Radiation therapy for head and neck cancers can affect taste, as can certain medications used in cancer treatment.
Smoking: Tobacco use can alter taste perception and damage taste buds.
Aging: As people age, their sense of taste can naturally decline.
Dry mouth: Reduced saliva production can affect taste, says the National Institute on Aging.
Ear, nose, and throat surgeries: Certain surgeries, especially those involving the ear, can sometimes affect the nerves responsible for taste.
Nerve injuries in the mouth or neck: Any injury to the nerves involved in taste can impair taste perception.

text_blocks.snippet: If you are experiencing a loss of taste, it's important to consult with a doctor to determine the underlying cause. Depending on the cause, treatment may involve addressing infections, adjusting medications, managing underlying medical conditions, or addressing nutritional deficiencies.
